facts.text: The flame robin is the largest of the red robins, measuring 12–14 cm long.
facts.quote: The largest of the red robins, the flame robin is 12–14 cm (4.7–5.5 in) long.

facts.text: The female is plainly coloured pale brown with a lighter buff underside, so the sexes look very different.
facts.quote: The female is plainly coloured—pale brown overall, and a lighter buff underneath.

facts.text: Its song has been described as the most musical of its genus.
facts.quote: Its song has been described as the most musical of its genus.

facts.text: It hunts by perching low and pouncing on insects, often returning repeatedly to a favourite perch to scan the leaf-litter.
facts.quote: Like all Australasian robins, the flame robin is a perch and pounce hunter, mainly eating insects, and often returning to a favourite low perch several times to stand erect and motionless, scanning the leaf-litter for more prey.

facts.text: One flame robin was seen pattering the ground with a foot to disturb insects, then snapping up any that emerged—a trick otherwise seen in waders.
facts.quote: In Deniliquin, a flame robin was observed holding one foot forward and pattering the ground repeatedly to disturb ground-dwelling insects, and then watching and snapping up any which emerged; this behaviour is otherwise seen in waders.

facts.text: It bashes larger prey against a hard surface to break it up, though such big victims make up only 0.5% of its prey over time.
facts.quote: The flame robin consumes small prey items whole, and bashes larger victims against a hard surface repeatedly to break up before eating. The latter group constitute only 0.5% of prey over time

facts.text: Males defend their territory with a breast-puffing display and a white spot display that highlights their white markings.
facts.quote: The flame robin deploys a number of agonistic displays, including a breast-puffing display where it puffs its breast feathers, and a white spot display where it puffs its feathers to accentuate its frontal white spot, white wing markings or white outer tail feathers.

facts.text: The breeding season runs from August to January, with one or two broods raised each year.
facts.quote: The breeding season is August to January with one or two broods raised.

facts.text: The female builds the nest alone, a neat deep cup of soft dry grass, moss and bark.
facts.quote: The nest is a neat, deep cup made of soft dry grass, moss, and bark.

facts.text: The male is easy to spot, with bright orange-red plumage on the throat, breast and abdomen.
facts.quote: The male is easily distinguished by the bright orange-red plumage of the throat, breast, and abdomen.
